title: Averaging mathematical overview
sections: Use a finite undirected graph. Squares have fixed real values; every circle has at least one neighbor and equals the arithmetic mean of all its neighbors, simultaneously. Each joined place counts once, including a place with value zero. This is a discrete harmonic function problem, not a procedure that conserves the total number of cubes.

For a connected component of circles, using only circle-to-circle joins, consider all squares directly joined to that group. If there is at least one, every circle value lies between the least and greatest of those boundary values. If one circle attains either extreme, all circles in that group and all its adjacent squares have that same value. Thus mixed boundary values force strict inequalities. Equality propagates through circles; it need not propagate through a fixed square into another group.

If every circle can reach a square, there is exactly one real-valued filling. The difference of two fillings is harmonic with zero boundary, so the maximum principle proves uniqueness. The finite linear system is then invertible, also giving existence. Values depend linearly on the boundary and are convex combinations of the relevant fixed values. Whole-number boundary values can require fractions. A connected component with only circles instead permits any constant value, so anchoring matters.

K-1 shares physical stacks, finds small collections and tests impossibility. Grades 2-3 balances several circles at once and compares extreme values. Grades 4-5 proves maximum propagation and, when ready for signed differences, uniqueness; separate tasks test unanchored components and fractional fillings.

Check proposed fillings at every circle. Several successful examples suggest a pattern; chasing a supposed extreme through a finite anchored group rules out every counterexample. A numerical guess alone does not prove uniqueness. Preserve the experiments before supplying the propagation argument; the longer proofs and all keyed solutions follow.
